DOMESTIC VIOLENCE RESTRAINING ORDER (REQUEST FOR ORDER) INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Pat Morgan

PETITIONER, RESPONDENT, RELATIONSHIP, AND INCIDENT DESCRIPTION
I, Jordan Lee, declare under penalty of perjury under the laws of the State of California that the following is true and correct. I am the petitioner in this matter. The respondent is Pat Morgan. The relationship between the petitioner and respondent, as described by the petitioner, is: Former spouse. On or about August 15, 2026, at or near 123 Main St., Sacramento, CA, the following occurred: On March 3, 2026, the respondent appeared outside the petitioner’s home and yelled threats for several minutes before leaving. Additional incidents, if any: On March 10, 2026, the respondent sent several threatening text messages to the petitioner. This declaration describes conduct alleged by the petitioner in connection with a request for a domestic violence restraining order under California Family Code section 6200 et seq. Whether the described relationship in fact falls within one of the categories listed in Family Code section 6211, and whether the described conduct in fact meets the statutory definition of abuse in Family Code section 6203, are determinations the court makes -- this declaration does not itself make either determination.

SCOPE OF THIS DOCUMENT AND DISTINCTION FROM CIVIL HARASSMENT ORDERS
California Family Code section 6200 states that Division 10 of the Family Code -- sections 6200 through 6460 -- may be cited as the Domestic Violence Prevention Act (DVPA). Code of Civil Procedure section 527.6(w) states that the civil harassment restraining order statute does not apply to any action or proceeding covered by the DVPA. The DVPA governs a restraining order between people who have one of the specific relationships listed in Family Code section 6211 (for example spouses, cohabitants, dating partners, co-parents, or certain close relatives), while Code of Civil Procedure section 527.6 governs harassment between people who do not have such a relationship. This document is an informational description of the DVPA process under Family Code section 6200 et seq. It states what the statute provides; it does not itself grant, deny, or constitute a restraining order. Only a court, applying this statutory process to a specific petition, can issue a restraining order.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "This division may be cited as the Domestic Violence Prevention Act."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 6200, the Domestic Violence Prevention Act's short title (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=6200.)
  "This section does not apply to any action or proceeding covered by Title 1.6C (commencing with Section 1788) of Part 4 of Division 3 of the Civil Code or by Division 10 (commencing with Section 6200) of the Family Code. This section does not preclude a petitioner from using other existing civil remedies."
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 527.6(w), civil harassment does not cover DVPA-governed proceedings (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=527.6)
  Known gap: This clause draws on two different, independently enacted California statutes -- Family Code section 6200 (the DVPA's short-title provision) and Code of Civil Procedure section 527.6(w) (the civil harassment statute's carve-out for DVPA-covered proceedings) -- rather than multiple subsections of a single section, so no single-section disclosure applies here. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how California itself distinguishes its domestic violence restraining order process from its civil harassment restraining order process -- not a claim about which state's law governs a specific petitioner's or respondent's relationship, or about whether an equivalent statutory distinction exists in any other state. Whether a specific relationship qualifies under Family Code section 6211 is a question of fact and law this clause does not resolve for any individual case.

WHO QUALIFIES FOR A DVPA RESTRAINING ORDER
Family Code section 6211 limits DVPA protection to abuse committed against specific categories of people: a spouse or former spouse; a cohabitant or former cohabitant, as defined in Family Code section 6209; a person the respondent is having or has had a dating or engagement relationship with; a person with whom the respondent has had a child, where a parentage presumption applies; a child of a party, or a child who is the subject of a parentage action, where that presumption applies; and any other person related to the respondent by consanguinity or affinity within the second degree. Family Code section 6209 defines a "cohabitant" as a person who regularly resides in the household, and a "former cohabitant" as a person who formerly regularly resided in the household.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  ""Domestic violence" is abuse perpetrated against any of the following persons: (a) A spouse or former spouse. (b) A cohabitant or former cohabitant, as defined in Section 6209. (c) A person with whom the respondent is having or has had a dating or engagement relationship. (d) A person with whom the respondent has had a child, where the presumption applies that the male parent is the father of the child of the female parent under the Uniform Parentage Act... (e) A child of a party or a child who is the subject of an action under the Uniform Parentage Act, where the presumption applies that the male parent is the father of the child to be protected. (f) Any other person related by consanguinity or affinity within the second degree."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 6211(a)-(f), the statutory list of qualifying relationships (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=6211.)
  ""Cohabitant" means a person who regularly resides in the household. "Former cohabitant" means a person who formerly regularly resided in the household."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 6209, the definition of cohabitant and former cohabitant (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=6209.)
  Known gap: Family Code section 6211's list and Family Code section 6209's definition are two different, independently added statutory sections, so no single-section disclosure applies here. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of which relationships California's DVPA covers -- not a claim about which state's law governs a specific pair of people, or about whether an equivalent relationship-based eligibility list exists in any other state's domestic violence statute. Whether a specific relationship falls within one of these categories -- for example, what makes a residence "regular" for cohabitant status, or what counts as a qualifying dating relationship -- has been the subject of considerable case law not reviewed for this clause; this clause states only the statutory categories, not how courts have applied them to particular facts.

STATUTORY DEFINITION OF "ABUSE" UNDER THE DVPA
Family Code section 6203(a) defines "abuse," for purposes of the Domestic Violence Prevention Act, as any of the following: intentionally or recklessly causing or attempting to cause bodily injury; sexual assault; placing a person in reasonable apprehension of imminent serious bodily injury to that person or to another; or engaging in any behavior that has been or could be enjoined under Family Code section 6320. Section 6203(b) states that abuse is not limited to the actual infliction of physical injury or assault.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "(a) For purposes of this act, "abuse" means any of the following: (1) To intentionally or recklessly cause or attempt to cause bodily injury. (2) Sexual assault. (3) To place a person in reasonable apprehension of imminent serious bodily injury to that person or to another. (4) To engage in any behavior that has been or could be enjoined pursuant to Section 6320. (b) Abuse is not limited to the actual infliction of physical injury or assault."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 6203(a)-(b), the four-category statutory definition of abuse (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=6203.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how California currently defines "abuse" under its Domestic Violence Prevention Act -- not a claim about which state's law governs a specific petitioner, respondent, or set of facts, and not a claim that another state's domestic violence statute defines abuse the same way. This is a single statutory subsection (§ 6203(a)-(b)); no additional independent source was found for this. Note for drafters: California's DVPA "abuse" definition is materially broader than a lay reading of the word -- it reaches conduct enjoinable under section 6320 (see the companion clause on disturbing the peace and coercive control), meaning physical violence is not required.

"DISTURBING THE PEACE" AND COERCIVE CONTROL
Family Code section 6320(a) authorizes a court to enjoin a party from molesting, attacking, striking, stalking, threatening, sexually assaulting, battering, harassing, contacting, coming within a specified distance of, or disturbing the peace of the other party, among other listed acts. Section 6320(c) defines "disturbing the peace of the other party," as used in subdivision (a), as conduct that, based on the totality of the circumstances, destroys the mental or emotional calm of the other party -- committed directly or indirectly, including through a third party or electronic means. This conduct expressly includes, but is not limited to, coercive control, defined as a pattern of behavior that in purpose or effect unreasonably interferes with a person's free will and personal liberty, with examples including isolating a party from support systems, depriving a party of basic necessities, monitoring a party's movements or finances, and reproductive coercion.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "The court may issue an ex parte order enjoining a party from molesting, attacking, striking, stalking, threatening, sexually assaulting, battering, credibly impersonating as described in Section 528.5 of the Penal Code, falsely personating as described in Section 529 of the Penal Code, harassing, telephoning, including, but not limited to, making annoying telephone calls as described in Section 653m of the Penal Code, destroying personal property, contacting, either directly or indirectly, by mail or otherwise, coming within a specified distance of, or disturbing the peace of the other party, and, in the discretion of the court, on a showing of good cause, of other named family or household members."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 6320(a), the categories of conduct a court may enjoin (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=6320.)
  "As used in subdivision (a), "disturbing the peace of the other party" refers to conduct that, based on the totality of the circumstances, destroys the mental or emotional calm of the other party. This conduct may be committed directly or indirectly, including through the use of a third party, and by any method or through any means including, but not limited to, telephone, online accounts, text messages, internet-connected devices... This conduct includes, but is not limited to, coercive control, which is a pattern of behavior that in purpose or effect unreasonably interferes with a person's free will and personal liberty. Examples of coercive control include, but are not limited to, unreasonably engaging in any of the following: (1) Isolating the other party from friends, relatives, or other sources of support. (2) Depriving the other party of basic necessities. (3) Controlling, regulating, or monitoring the other party's movements, communications, daily behavior, finances, economic resources, or access to services. (4) Compelling the other party by force, threat of force, or intimidation... (5) Engaging in reproductive coercion..."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 6320(c), the statutory definition of "disturbing the peace," including coercive control (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=6320.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of what California's DVPA currently reaches under "disturbing the peace" and coercive control -- not a claim about which state's law governs a specific petitioner or respondent, and many states have no equivalent coercive-control provision at all. Family Code section 6320, subdivisions (a) and (c), are provisions of a single California statutory section; this is a single statutory section (§ 6320(a), (c)); no additional independent source was found for this. The coercive-control language quoted here is the section's current text, in effect as amended by Stats. 2025, Ch. 676 (SB 50), effective January 1, 2026; this research confirmed the current text directly but did not independently fetch and compare an archived pre-2025 version, so while coercive control is widely reported to have first entered this subdivision through a 2020 amendment, that specific origination is not independently confirmed here -- only that the concept, with additional examples (including reproductive coercion and immigration-status-based threats), is part of the section as currently in force.

THE STANDARD A COURT APPLIES
Family Code section 6300(a) allows a court to issue a DVPA restraining order where an affidavit or testimony, and any additional information provided under Family Code section 6306, shows to the court's satisfaction reasonable proof of a past act or acts of abuse -- and the court may issue the order based solely on the petitioner's own affidavit or testimony. Family Code section 6301(d), a separate subdivision within the same statutory part, adds that the length of time since the most recent act of abuse is not, by itself, determinative, and directs the court to consider the totality of the circumstances in deciding whether to grant or deny the petition.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "An order may be issued under this part to restrain any person for the purpose specified in Section 6220, if an affidavit or testimony and any additional information provided to the court pursuant to Section 6306, shows, to the satisfaction of the court, reasonable proof of a past act or acts of abuse. The court may issue an order under this part based solely on the affidavit or testimony of the person requesting the restraining order."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 6300(a), reasonable proof of a past act or acts of abuse (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=6300.)
  "The length of time since the most recent act of abuse is not, by itself, determinative. The court shall consider the totality of the circumstances in determining whether to grant or deny a petition for relief."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 6301(d), the totality-of-the-circumstances standard (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=6301.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute (Cal. Fam. Code §§ 6300 and 6301), used as real evidence of the standard California's DVPA currently applies -- not a claim about which state's law governs a specific petition, or that this is the applicable standard nationwide. Correction to an initial research assumption: the "totality of the circumstances" language is often associated with section 6300 in older secondary sources and in casual research shorthand, but the current, directly-fetched text of section 6300 (as amended by Stats. 2024, Ch. 648 (AB 2024), effective January 1, 2025) does not contain that phrase -- it appears instead in the current text of the separate section 6301(d) (as amended by Stats. 2024, Ch. 652 (SB 554), effective January 1, 2025), which also states that the passage of time since the last abusive act is not by itself determinative. Because sections 6300 and 6301 are two different, independently amended statutory sections rather than subsections of one section, no single-section disclosure applies to this pairing; this clause cites both directly rather than assuming the older single-section attribution.

TEMPORARY (EX PARTE) ORDERS AND HOW LONG A PERMANENT ORDER LASTS
Family Code section 6326 states that an ex parte DVPA order must be issued or denied the same day the application is submitted to the court, or the next day of judicial business if filed too late in the day for effective review, and that a petition for an ex parte order cannot be denied solely because the other party lacked notice. For a permanent order issued after notice and a hearing, Family Code section 6345(a) allows the personal conduct, stay-away, and residence exclusion provisions to last up to five years, and permits the order to be renewed -- without any showing of further abuse since the original order -- for five or more additional years, or permanently, at the court's discretion. Section 6345(c) provides that if the order's expiration date is not stated on the form, the order defaults to a three-year duration from issuance.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "An ex parte order under this article shall be issued or denied on the same day that the application is submitted to the court, unless the application is filed too late in the day to permit effective review, in which case the order shall be issued or denied on the next day of judicial business in sufficient time for the order to be filed that day with the clerk of the court. A petition for an ex parte order pursuant to this article shall not be denied solely because the other party was not provided with notice."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 6326, the same-day ex parte order mechanism (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=6326.)
  "In the discretion of the court, the personal conduct, stay-away, and residence exclusion orders contained in a court order issued after notice and a hearing under this article may have a duration of not more than five years... These orders may be renewed, upon the request of a party, either for five or more years, or permanently, at the discretion of the court, without a showing of further abuse since the issuance of the original order."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 6345(a), duration and renewal of a permanent order (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=6345.)
  "The failure to state the expiration date on the face of the form creates an order with a duration of three years from the date of issuance."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 6345(c), the default three-year duration when no expiration date is stated (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=6345.)
  Known gap: Family Code section 6326 is a separate statutory section from Family Code section 6345, so no single-section disclosure applies to that pairing; but section 6345's subdivisions (a) and (c), cited together above, are both provisions of one statutory section (§ 6345), so this is a single statutory section for that portion; no additional independent source was found for the duration figures. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's own ex parte mechanism and permanent-order duration rules -- not a claim about which state's law governs a specific petition, and not a claim that an equivalent ex parte or duration scheme exists in any other state. This clause does not restate the full hearing-scheduling mechanism for an ex parte DVPA order (Family Code section 6327 cross-references the general temporary restraining order provisions commencing at Code of Civil Procedure section 240, rather than stating its own fixed number of days the way Code of Civil Procedure section 527.6(f)-(g) does for civil harassment orders), so this document does not state a specific day count for how long a DVPA temporary order remains in effect before the hearing -- that figure was not independently confirmed with a clean, self-contained citation and is not guessed at here. Notably, a DVPA order's renewal is not capped the way a civil harassment order's renewal is: section 6345(a) allows renewal "for five or more years, or permanently," which is broader than the civil harassment statute's cap of one renewal for up to five additional years.

FIREARM RELINQUISHMENT CONSEQUENCE
Family Code section 6389(a) states that a person subject to a DVPA protective order, as defined in Family Code section 6218, shall not own, possess, purchase, or receive a firearm or ammunition while the order is in effect, and that doing so is punishable under Penal Code section 29825. Section 6389(c)(1)-(2) requires the court, upon issuing a protective order, to order the respondent to relinquish any firearm or ammunition in the respondent's immediate possession or control; relinquishment must occur immediately to a requesting law enforcement officer upon service, or, if no such request is made, within 24 hours by surrender to local law enforcement or sale, transfer, or storage with a licensed gun dealer, with a receipt filed with both the court and the serving law enforcement agency within 48 hours.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "A person subject to a protective order, as defined in Section 6218, shall not own, possess, purchase, or receive a firearm or ammunition while that protective order is in effect. A person who owns, possesses, purchases, or receives, or attempts to purchase or receive, a firearm or ammunition while the protective order is in effect is punishable pursuant to Section 29825 of the Penal Code."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 6389(a), the prohibition on firearm ownership or possession while an order is in effect (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=6389.)
  "(1) Upon issuance of a protective order, as defined in Section 6218, the court shall order the respondent to relinquish any firearm or ammunition in the respondent's immediate possession or control or subject to the respondent's immediate possession or control. (2) The relinquishment ordered pursuant to paragraph (1) shall occur by immediately surrendering the firearm or ammunition in a safe manner, upon request of a law enforcement officer, to the control of the officer, after being served with the protective order... Alternatively, if a request is not made by a law enforcement officer, the relinquishment shall occur within 24 hours of being served with the order, by either surrendering the firearm or ammunition in a safe manner to the control of local law enforcement officials, or by selling, transferring, or relinquishing for storage... to a licensed gun dealer..."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 6389(c)(1)-(2), the mandatory relinquishment procedure (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=6389.)
  Known gap: Family Code section 6389, subdivisions (a) and (c)(1)-(2), are provisions of a single California statutory section; no additional independent source was found for this. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a specific, checkable consequence that attaches to a California DVPA protective order -- not a claim about which state's law governs a specific respondent, and not a claim that firearm relinquishment is a feature of every state's domestic violence restraining order. This consequence is distinct from a civil harassment order under Code of Civil Procedure section 527.6, which does not carry an equivalent statutory firearm-relinquishment requirement. Section 6389 was substantially amended effective January 1, 2026 (as added by Stats. 2024, Ch. 544, then amended by Stats. 2025, Ch. 241 (SB 857)); this clause quotes the section as currently in force. This clause does not restate the section's narrow work-related and peace-officer exemption procedures under subdivisions (h) and (i), which involve separate court findings and psychological evaluation requirements not summarized here.

expectedJSON.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of what California's DVPA currently reaches under "disturbing the peace" and coercive control -- not a claim about which state's law governs a specific petitioner or respondent, and many states have no equivalent coercive-control provision at all. Family Code section 6320, subdivisions (a) and (c), are provisions of a single California statutory section; this is a single statutory section (§ 6320(a), (c)); no additional independent source was found for this. The coercive-control language quoted here is the section's current text, in effect as amended by Stats. 2025, Ch. 676 (SB 50), effective January 1, 2026; this research confirmed the current text directly but did not independently fetch and compare an archived pre-2025 version, so while coercive control is widely reported to have first entered this subdivision through a 2020 amendment, that specific origination is not independently confirmed here -- only that the concept, with additional examples (including reproductive coercion and immigration-status-based threats), is part of the section as currently in force.

expectedJSON.body: Family Code section 6300(a) allows a court to issue a DVPA restraining order where an affidavit or testimony, and any additional information provided under Family Code section 6306, shows to the court's satisfaction reasonable proof of a past act or acts of abuse -- and the court may issue the order based solely on the petitioner's own affidavit or testimony. Family Code section 6301(d), a separate subdivision within the same statutory part, adds that the length of time since the most recent act of abuse is not, by itself, determinative, and directs the court to consider the totality of the circumstances in deciding whether to grant or deny the petition.

citations.cite: reasonable proof of a past act or acts of abuse
citations.quote: An order may be issued under this part to restrain any person for the purpose specified in Section 6220, if an affidavit or testimony and any additional information provided to the court pursuant to Section 6306, shows, to the satisfaction of the court, reasonable proof of a past act or acts of abuse. The court may issue an order under this part based solely on the affidavit or testimony of the person requesting the restraining order.

The length of time since the most recent act of abuse is not, by itself, determinative. The court shall consider the totality of the circumstances in determining whether to grant or deny a petition for relief.

expectedJSON.gap: This is one state's statute (Cal. Fam. Code §§ 6300 and 6301), used as real evidence of the standard California's DVPA currently applies -- not a claim about which state's law governs a specific petition, or that this is the applicable standard nationwide. Correction to an initial research assumption: the "totality of the circumstances" language is often associated with section 6300 in older secondary sources and in casual research shorthand, but the current, directly-fetched text of section 6300 (as amended by Stats. 2024, Ch. 648 (AB 2024), effective January 1, 2025) does not contain that phrase -- it appears instead in the current text of the separate section 6301(d) (as amended by Stats. 2024, Ch. 652 (SB 554), effective January 1, 2025), which also states that the passage of time since the last abusive act is not by itself determinative. Because sections 6300 and 6301 are two different, independently amended statutory sections rather than subsections of one section, no single-section disclosure applies to this pairing; this clause cites both directly rather than assuming the older single-section attribution.

expectedJSON.body: Family Code section 6326 states that an ex parte DVPA order must be issued or denied the same day the application is submitted to the court, or the next day of judicial business if filed too late in the day for effective review, and that a petition for an ex parte order cannot be denied solely because the other party lacked notice. For a permanent order issued after notice and a hearing, Family Code section 6345(a) allows the personal conduct, stay-away, and residence exclusion provisions to last up to five years, and permits the order to be renewed -- without any showing of further abuse since the original order -- for five or more additional years, or permanently, at the court's discretion. Section 6345(c) provides that if the order's expiration date is not stated on the form, the order defaults to a three-year duration from issuance.

citations.cite: the same-day ex parte order mechanism
citations.quote: An ex parte order under this article shall be issued or denied on the same day that the application is submitted to the court, unless the application is filed too late in the day to permit effective review, in which case the order shall be issued or denied on the next day of judicial business in sufficient time for the order to be filed that day with the clerk of the court. A petition for an ex parte order pursuant to this article shall not be denied solely because the other party was not provided with notice.

citations.cite: duration and renewal of a permanent order
citations.quote: In the discretion of the court, the personal conduct, stay-away, and residence exclusion orders contained in a court order issued after notice and a hearing under this article may have a duration of not more than five years... These orders may be renewed, upon the request of a party, either for five or more years, or permanently, at the discretion of the court, without a showing of further abuse since the issuance of the original order.

citations.cite: the default three-year duration when no expiration date is stated
citations.quote: The failure to state the expiration date on the face of the form creates an order with a duration of three years from the date of issuance.

expectedJSON.gap: Family Code section 6326 is a separate statutory section from Family Code section 6345, so no single-section disclosure applies to that pairing; but section 6345's subdivisions (a) and (c), cited together above, are both provisions of one statutory section (§ 6345), so this is a single statutory section for that portion; no additional independent source was found for the duration figures. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's own ex parte mechanism and permanent-order duration rules -- not a claim about which state's law governs a specific petition, and not a claim that an equivalent ex parte or duration scheme exists in any other state. This clause does not restate the full hearing-scheduling mechanism for an ex parte DVPA order (Family Code section 6327 cross-references the general temporary restraining order provisions commencing at Code of Civil Procedure section 240, rather than stating its own fixed number of days the way Code of Civil Procedure section 527.6(f)-(g) does for civil harassment orders), so this document does not state a specific day count for how long a DVPA temporary order remains in effect before the hearing -- that figure was not independently confirmed with a clean, self-contained citation and is not guessed at here. Notably, a DVPA order's renewal is not capped the way a civil harassment order's renewal is: section 6345(a) allows renewal "for five or more years, or permanently," which is broader than the civil harassment statute's cap of one renewal for up to five additional years.

expectedJSON.body: Family Code section 6389(a) states that a person subject to a DVPA protective order, as defined in Family Code section 6218, shall not own, possess, purchase, or receive a firearm or ammunition while the order is in effect, and that doing so is punishable under Penal Code section 29825. Section 6389(c)(1)-(2) requires the court, upon issuing a protective order, to order the respondent to relinquish any firearm or ammunition in the respondent's immediate possession or control; relinquishment must occur immediately to a requesting law enforcement officer upon service, or, if no such request is made, within 24 hours by surrender to local law enforcement or sale, transfer, or storage with a licensed gun dealer, with a receipt filed with both the court and the serving law enforcement agency within 48 hours.

citations.cite: the prohibition on firearm ownership or possession while an order is in effect
citations.quote: A person subject to a protective order, as defined in Section 6218, shall not own, possess, purchase, or receive a firearm or ammunition while that protective order is in effect. A person who owns, possesses, purchases, or receives, or attempts to purchase or receive, a firearm or ammunition while the protective order is in effect is punishable pursuant to Section 29825 of the Penal Code.

(1) Upon issuance of a protective order, as defined in Section 6218, the court shall order the respondent to relinquish any firearm or ammunition in the respondent's immediate possession or control or subject to the respondent's immediate possession or control. (2) The relinquishment ordered pursuant to paragraph (1) shall occur by immediately surrendering the firearm or ammunition in a safe manner, upon request of a law enforcement officer, to the control of the officer, after being served with the protective order... Alternatively, if a request is not made by a law enforcement officer, the relinquishment shall occur within 24 hours of being served with the order, by either surrendering the firearm or ammunition in a safe manner to the control of local law enforcement officials, or by selling, transferring, or relinquishing for storage... to a licensed gun dealer...

expectedJSON.gap: Family Code section 6389, subdivisions (a) and (c)(1)-(2), are provisions of a single California statutory section; no additional independent source was found for this. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a specific, checkable consequence that attaches to a California DVPA protective order -- not a claim about which state's law governs a specific respondent, and not a claim that firearm relinquishment is a feature of every state's domestic violence restraining order. This consequence is distinct from a civil harassment order under Code of Civil Procedure section 527.6, which does not carry an equivalent statutory firearm-relinquishment requirement. Section 6389 was substantially amended effective January 1, 2026 (as added by Stats. 2024, Ch. 544, then amended by Stats. 2025, Ch. 241 (SB 857)); this clause quotes the section as currently in force. This clause does not restate the section's narrow work-related and peace-officer exemption procedures under subdivisions (h) and (i), which involve separate court findings and psychological evaluation requirements not summarized here.
